To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the RAD9 gene is essential for cell cycle arrest of the cdc mutants that arrest in the late S and G2 phases of the cell division cycle and that the RAD9 and the RAD17 genes are essential for delay in the S phase after X or UV-irradiaction of cells.

(1) the RAD9 checkpoint arrests cell division only after DNA replication is complete or nearly complete and (2) the RAD9 gene is required for the phase-specific arrest of four cdc mutants that arrest in the late S phase or G2 phase and are defective in DNA replication enzymes and for the delay in the G phase of X- or UV-radiated cells.
RAD9 is required for arrest of four cdc mutants in late S/G2, but not for arrest of eight other mutants.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the function of genes involved in the control of cell division in yeast.
the function of a cell cycle checkpoint in yeast.
the molecular mechanisms that regulate the cell cycle.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the RAD9 and the RAD17 genes function together to ensure that the cell cycle is halted until the DNA damage is repaired.
the RAD9 and the RAD17 gene products are essential for cell cycle control in the late S-G2 phase in response to DNA damage.
the RAD9 and possibly the RAD17 genes are required for cell cycle arrest in response to DNA lesions that occur during late S phase and/or G2 phase.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the RAD9 gene is essential for cell cycle arrest in the S/G2 phase of the cell cycle when DNA damage is present.
the RAD9 and the RAD17 genes are required for the function of a cell cycle checkpoint that is activated by DNA lesions and that arrests cell division in the late S-G2 phase.

the function of the checkpoint in cdc mutants is to prevent mitosis when there is incomplete DNA replication or DNA damage, and that the RAD9 gene is required to arrest the cell division of the four cdc mutants when DNA damage occurs during the late S/G _{2} phase.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the function of the Rad9 checkpoint is phase specific and signal specific.
the RAD9 gene is required for cell cycle arrest of four cdc mutants, which indicates that the function of RAD9 is cell cycle phase- and signal-specific.

there are two distinct types of cell division checkpoints in eucaryotes: one that arrests the cell cycle when DNA damage is detected, and another that arrests the cell division cycle when DNA replication is not complete.
